blocks.text: Making a daily timetable is an example of computational thinking. Cooking a recipe uses step-by-step instructions. Planning a trip includes breaking tasks into smaller parts. Sorting books by subject or size shows pattern recognition. Fixing a mobile phone problem uses logical thinking. Managing money needs planning and decision making. Playing strategy games requires thinking ahead. All these activities use computational thinking in real life (as shown in Figure 2.1).

blocks.alt: Under the title Computational Thinking in Daily Life, four numbered panels sit along an arrow pointing right: 1. Decomposition, Break Down the Problem (one big box split into four small boxes); 2. Pattern Recognition, Find Patterns (a circle-square pair repeating, with a question mark for the next shape); 3. Abstraction, Focus on What's Important (many shapes poured into a funnel, one shape comes out); 4. Algorithm Design, Create Step-by-Step Solution (a numbered list of steps with a tick).
